msgs.quest_init: The Sun is the center of our solar system, containing 99.86% of its mass. The eight planets, from Mercury near the Sun to Neptune far away, each have unique characteristics. Remembering their names and order is the first step to understanding the solar system.
msgs.quest_size_sort: Jupiter is the largest planet at 139,820 km in diameter — 11 times Earth. Saturn follows, while Mercury is the smallest. The size differences between planets are far greater than you can imagine.
msgs.quest_eccentric: Planetary orbits are not perfect circles. Mercury has the highest eccentricity (0.2056) — its perihelion is 23 million km closer than its aphelion. Set eccentricity to ×4 and Mercury's ellipse becomes very visible.
msgs.quest_retrograde: Most planets rotate west to east, but Venus and Uranus are exceptions. Venus rotates extremely slowly in reverse — the Sun rises in the west there. Uranus spins on its side with a 97.77° tilt.
msgs.quest_earth_scale: This is the real size of planets in the universe. At ×1 scale, even Jupiter is a tiny dot, and Earth is nearly invisible. That's why the scene defaults to ×1200 — without it you couldn't interact at all. The scale of the cosmos is beyond imagination.
msgs.quest_saturn: Saturn's rings are made of ice particles and rock fragments. They span about 280,000 km (roughly 3/4 of the Earth-Moon distance) but are only about 10 meters thick — a vast, paper-thin disk.
msgs.quest_asteroid: The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter (2.2~3.2 AU) and contains millions of asteroids. But their total mass is less than 4% of the Moon's — though it looks dense, it's actually extremely empty.
msgs.quest_comet: Comets originate from the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud at the edge of the solar system, with extremely elliptical orbits. As they approach the Sun, surface ice sublimates to form a coma and tail — always pointing away from the Sun.
msgs.quest_graduate: Congratulations on completing the journey! You now understand the solar system's composition, planetary scales, orbital shapes, and rotation diversity. The universe is vast, but you've taken the first step.
msgs.quest_quiz_master: Knowledge builds one step at a time. You've mastered the basics of the solar system — keep challenging yourself with more questions.
msgs.quest_speedster: With time speed at ×100, you can watch planets race along their orbits. A year on Saturn is about 29.5 Earth years, Jupiter 11.86 years, but Mercury only needs 88 days — the inner planets sure move fast!
msgs.quest_moon: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite, 3,474 km in diameter, averaging about 384,000 km away. This distance is large enough to fit all the planets in the solar system lined up in a row. The Moon's gravity stabilizes Earth's axial tilt, giving us stable seasons.
msgs.quest_neptune: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun, averaging 30.1 AU away. It glows blue and has winds reaching 2,100 km/h — the fastest in the solar system. It was the first planet discovered through mathematical prediction rather than direct observation, in 1846.
